title: Keenen v. Russ
description: Whether the Energy Discrimination Elimination Act of 2022 (EDEA) is constitutional when applied to the Oklahoma Public Employees Retirement System (OPERS), with the plaintiff arguing it violates the Oklahoma Constitution's exclusive purpose clause for public retirement systems, and the defendant arguing it is constitutional and protects state funds by ensuring investments are solely for financial reasons.
plaintiff_argument: Keenan argued the EDEA was unconstitutional, specifically violating Okla. Const. Art. XXIII, §12, by creating a 'dual purpose' for OPERS's investment decisions beyond the exclusive purpose of providing benefits, refunds, investment management, and administrative expenses. He sought an injunction to prevent the Treasurer from enforcing the Act against OPERS.
defendant_argument: The Treasurer argued the EDEA was constitutional, designed to protect state funds by ensuring private entities managing those funds do not subordinate fiduciary duty to political goals, and that the Act makes providing benefits and investment management more effective. He also argued Keenan lacked standing.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the District Court's summary judgment, ruling that the Energy Discrimination Elimination Act of 2022 is unconstitutional in its entirety when applied to the Oklahoma Public Employees Retirement System and permanently enjoined the Treasurer from enforcing it against OPERS.

title: Tobacco Settlement Endowment Trust Fund v. Stitt
description: Whether HB 2783, which changes the terms of the Tobacco Settlement Endowment Trust Fund (TSET) Board of Directors from fixed seven-year terms to at-will terms, violates the Oklahoma Constitution's requirement for fixed seven-year terms.
plaintiff_argument: The Tobacco Settlement Endowment Trust Fund (TSET) argues that HB 2783 is unconstitutional because it removes the Article X Section 40(D) requirement that TSET directors serve staggered fixed seven-year terms, replacing them with at-will terms.
defendant_argument: The respondents argue that the Legislature has the authority to create a removal mechanism for TSET directors, that the existing fixed-term structure is preserved, and that the Constitution does not explicitly prohibit the Legislature from altering appointment requirements by statute.
decision_outcome: The court found HB 2783 unconstitutional and granted declaratory relief, affirming that TSET directors must serve staggered fixed seven-year terms as mandated by the Constitution.

title: White v. Stitt
description: Whether Senate Bill 632, which establishes business court divisions and an appointment process for judges, is constitutional under Article VII, Section 9 of the Oklahoma Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that Senate Bill 632 is unconstitutional because it violates Article VII, Section 9 of the Oklahoma Constitution by circumventing the election of business court judges, and that they have standing as taxpayers and registered voters whose rights are infringed.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that Senate Bill 632 is constitutional, that business court judges are not district judges and thus not subject to election requirements, and that the plaintiffs lacked standing and he was not a proper party to the dispute.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that Senate Bill 632 is an unconstitutional violation of Article VII, Section 9 of the Oklahoma Constitution, voiding the Act in its entirety, and denied the Governor's Motion to Dismiss.

title: Donaldson v. City of El Reno
description: Whether applying the current residency restrictions to a sex offender who became subject to SORA prior to the enactment or amendment of the law violates the ex post facto clause of either the United States Constitution or the Oklahoma Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: Donaldson argued that applying the current residency restrictions retroactively violates ex post facto laws, and the law in effect at his conviction should apply, which did not prohibit residing near parks.
defendant_argument: The City of El Reno argued that the residency restrictions are nonpunitive civil regulations and can be applied retroactively without violating ex post facto laws.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the residency restrictions for sex offenders do not amount to punishment and can be applied retroactively to Donaldson without violating ex post facto clauses, thereby reversing the trial court's judgment.

title: Connor v. Oklahoma
description: Whether the Governmental Tort Claims Act's (GTCA) notice provisions apply when an individual sues a governmental entity under Oklahoma's anti-discrimination statutes (OADA).
plaintiff_argument: Conner argued that the GTCA excludes coverage for actions under the OADA because OADA covers intentional torts outside the GTCA's scope, and that the OADA, as a more specific statute, should control over the GTCA due to material conflicts.
defendant_argument: The OESC argued that Conner failed to comply with the GTCA's mandatory notice provisions, which are a jurisdictional requirement for maintaining a cause of action against a governmental entity.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the trial court's ruling, finding no material conflict between the GTCA and OADA regarding notice provisions, and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion that GTCA notice is required.

title: Cherokee Nation  v. U.S. Department of the Interior
description: Whether the Attorney General of Oklahoma can assume control of the defense of the state's interests in a federal case where the Governor is a named defendant and has already retained counsel, over the Governor's objection.
plaintiff_argument: The Plaintiff tribes argue the gaming compacts were not lawfully entered into by the Governor and violated Oklahoma law, precluding federal "no action" approval. The Attorney General, aligning with the plaintiff tribes' stance, argues the compacts are invalid under Oklahoma law and therefore the Governor's defense of them in federal court is inconsistent with state law, giving the AG power to take over.
defendant_argument: Governor Stitt argues that he has the constitutional and statutory authority to retain his own counsel to defend the state's interests, and the Attorney General cannot assume control over his objection, especially since the compacts' federal approval is valid and state law issues can be severed.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the Attorney General cannot take and assume control of the defense of the state's interests in the federal case over the Governor's objection, affirming the Governor's right to use his chosen counsel.

title: State v. Velasquez
description: Whether the exclusionary rule is an appropriate remedy for a violation of the 'knock and announce' rule (22 O.S.2021, § 1228) during the execution of a search warrant, with the State arguing it is not an appropriate remedy and the Appellee arguing it is.
plaintiff_argument: The State argues the District Court abused its discretion by applying the Exclusionary Rule as a remedy for a statutory violation of the 'knock and announce' rule, suppressing all evidence seized pursuant to a valid search warrant.
defendant_argument: The Appellee argues that the officers' illegal execution of the search warrant, violating the 'knock and announce' rule, warranted the suppression of all seized evidence under the Exclusionary Rule.
decision_outcome: The State's appeal is granted, the District Court's order granting the motion to quash the bindover is reversed, and the case is remanded for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

title: Independent School District No. 12 v. State of Oklahoma
description: Whether the State Board of Education, State Department of Education, and State Superintendent of Public Instruction may control the selection of supplemental books and educational materials by local school boards for school libraries, with the plaintiff arguing against state control and the defendant arguing for state authority to enforce rules.
plaintiff_argument: The Edmond Public Schools argued that the State Board of Education lacked statutory authority to adopt and enforce library censorship rules, and that local school boards possess the discretion to select library books based on local community standards.
defendant_argument: The State Board of Education argued that its proposed rules for school library media programs were validly promulgated under its established authority, complied with the Administrative Procedures Act, and that the Governor had the authority to approve them.
decision_outcome: The court issued a writ of prohibition against the State Board of Education, State Department of Education, and State Superintendent of Public Instruction, directing them to dismiss enforcement proceedings against the Edmond School District regarding library book selection, and denied the petitioner's request for declaratory and injunctive relief.

title: Jackson County Emergency Medical Service District v. Kirkland
description: Whether the Jackson County Emergency Medical Services District (JCEMSD) is entitled to governmental immunity under the Governmental Tort Claims Act (GTCA) and if the GTCA precludes recovery for a plaintiff who has already received workers' compensation benefits.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the medical district is not a governmental entity and therefore not entitled to governmental immunity under the GTCA, meaning the GTCA's preclusion of recovery for workers' compensation recipients does not apply.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the JCEMSD is entitled to governmental immunity under the GTCA, and the GTCA precludes recovery because the plaintiff already received workers' compensation benefits.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court assumed original jurisdiction and granted the writ of prohibition, ruling that the medical district is subject to governmental immunity under the GTCA, and the lawsuit is precluded because workers' compensation benefits were already awarded.

title: Drummond  v. Statewide Virtual Charter Schoolboard
description: Whether the contract between the Oklahoma Statewide Virtual Charter School Board and St. Isidore of Seville Catholic Virtual School, a religious virtual charter school, violates state and federal law and is unconstitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the contract violates the Oklahoma Constitution, the Oklahoma Charter Schools Act, and the federal Establishment Clause because St. Isidore is a public school and must be nonsectarian, thus public funds cannot be used to establish or fund a religious institution.
defendant_argument: The Charter School Board and St. Isidore argued that St. Isidore is a private corporation, not a public school, and that the contract does not violate state or federal law. They contended that denying St. Isidore the right to operate as a charter school solely because it is religious violates the Free Exercise Clause.
decision_outcome: The court ruled in favor of the State, granting a writ of mandamus and declaratory relief, directing the Charter School Board to rescind its contract with St. Isidore, finding it violates state and federal law and is unconstitutional.

title: State Chamber of Oklahoma v. Cobbs
description: Whether Initiative Petition No. 446 is legally sufficient and constitutional to proceed to a vote by the people.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argues that Initiative Petition No. 446 is unconstitutional due to non-delegation doctrine violations, is not capable of correction by severance, and has a faulty gist, thus it should not proceed to a vote.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that Initiative Petition No. 446 is legally sufficient and does not clearly or manifestly violate the Oklahoma or United States Constitution, and therefore should be allowed to proceed to signature gathering and a vote.
decision_outcome: The court assumed original jurisdiction, denied all relief, and ruled that Initiative Petition No. 446 is legally sufficient and may proceed with signature gathering.

title: Deo v. Parish
description: Whether Oklahoma state courts have subject matter jurisdiction over crimes committed by an Indian in Indian Country, or if such jurisdiction is preempted by federal law, and whether the petitioner's claim was waived.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Billy Zane Deo, argued that the Okfuskee County District Court lacked subject matter jurisdiction over his cases because his crimes occurred in Indian Country and he is an enrolled member of the Muscogee Nation, citing McGirt v. Oklahoma.
defendant_argument: The defendant, The Honorable Lawrence Parish, implicitly argued that the state court retained jurisdiction, or that the petitioner's claim was waived due to his failure to raise it prior to entering his pleas.
decision_outcome: The court denied the Petitioner's application for an extraordinary writ of mandamus and remanded the matter to the Okfuskee County District Court for further proceedings.

title: Treat v. Stitt
description: Whether the Oklahoma Legislature's passage of S.B. 26x and H.B. 1005x, which extend State-Tribal compacts, is constitutional, specifically regarding the special session process, exceeding the session's call, and infringing on the Governor's authority to negotiate compacts.
plaintiff_argument: The Governor argued that the bills are invalid because they were passed during an unconstitutional concurrent special session, exceeded the scope of the special session's call, and infringed upon his exclusive constitutional and statutory authority to negotiate State-Tribal compacts.
defendant_argument: The Legislature contended that the concurrent special session was constitutional, the bills fell within the scope of the special session's call as they relate to budget-related funds, and the Governor's authority to negotiate compacts is statutory and subject to legislative limitation, not constitutional.
decision_outcome: The court denied the Governor's request for declaratory relief, upholding the validity of Senate Bill 26x and House Bill 1005x.

title: Oklahoma Call for Reproductive Justice v. Drummond
description: Whether three Oklahoma Acts (H.B. 1904, S.B. 778, and S.B. 779) that restrict abortion access violate the Oklahoma Constitution's due process clause by placing undue burdens on a woman's right to terminate a pregnancy when necessary to preserve her life.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the three Acts severely and intentionally restrict access to abortions, are unrelated to patient health, and place undue burdens on a woman's constitutional right to terminate a pregnancy when necessary to preserve her life, thus violating the Oklahoma Constitution.
defendant_argument: The defendants asserted that the three Acts are designed to benefit women's health and are therefore constitutional.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the trial court's order denying a temporary injunction against the enforcement of the three Acts and directed the trial court to grant a temporary injunction, remanding the matter for further proceedings on the merits.

title: Berkson v. State ex rel. Askins
description: Whether 28 O.S. § 86, which imposes a $10 Lengthy Trial Fund Fee on attorneys filing civil cases while exempting certain litigants, is an unconstitutional special law.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Berkson, argued that the Lengthy Trial Fund fee statute is an unconstitutional special law because it creates impermissible classes of similarly situated litigants by exempting pro se litigants without a logical connection to the likelihood of a lengthy trial.
defendant_argument: The defendants, the State of Oklahoma and District Court Clerks, argued that Berkson lacked standing to bring the action and that 28 O.S. § 86 is not an unconstitutional special law, as the legislative classification is reasonable.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the District Court's dismissal, concluding that the plaintiff's petition failed to state a claim that 28 O.S. § 86 is an unconstitutional special law.

title: Oklahoma Call for Reproductive Justice v. State
description: Whether Oklahoma's S.B. 1503 and H.B. 4327, which criminalize abortion, are constitutional under the Oklahoma Constitution, with petitioners arguing they are unconstitutional and the state arguing they are constitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners argued that S.B. 1503 and H.B. 4327 are unconstitutional as they prohibit abortion in violation of the Oklahoma Constitution, infringing on a pregnant woman's inherent right to terminate a pregnancy when necessary to preserve her life.
defendant_argument: The State of Oklahoma implicitly argued that S.B. 1503 and H.B. 4327 are constitutional and enforceable.
decision_outcome: The court assumed original jurisdiction, granted declaratory relief finding both S.B. 1503 and H.B. 4327 unconstitutional and unenforceable, but denied the petitioners' request for injunctive relief and writ of prohibition.

title: Schlumberger Tech. Corp. v. Paredes
description: Whether a workers' compensation claim is timely filed if it is within one year from the date of injury or six months from the last payment of benefits, with the claimant receiving the benefit of whichever period is longer, or if the shorter period applies when benefits have been paid.
plaintiff_argument: Paredes argued that his claim was timely filed within one year of the injury and that the statute of limitations should be interpreted to give the claimant the benefit of the longer period (one year from injury or six months from last benefit payment, whichever is greater), as Schlumberger's interpretation would raise constitutional due process concerns due to lack of notice.
defendant_argument: Schlumberger argued that the statute of limitations, after a 2019 amendment, means a claimant has either one year from the date of injury or six months from the date of the last issuance of benefits, whichever is lesser, because the phrase "whichever is greater" was removed from the statute.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Workers' Compensation Commission's order, ruling that Erasmo Paredes's claim was timely filed and not barred by the statute of limitations.

title: Oklahoma Call for Reproductive Justice v. Drummond
description: Whether the Oklahoma Constitution protects a woman's right to terminate a pregnancy, and if two state statutes criminalizing abortion are constitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The Oklahoma Constitution protects a woman's inherent right to terminate a pregnancy, making the challenged statutes criminalizing abortion unconstitutional.
defendant_argument: The challenged statutes criminalizing abortion are constitutional, and the Oklahoma Constitution does not protect a right to abortion.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the Oklahoma Constitution protects a limited right to terminate a pregnancy to preserve the woman's life, found one statute (63 O.S.Supp. 2022, § 1-731.4) unconstitutional and unenforceable, and upheld another statute (21 O.S. 2021, § 861) as constitutional because it allows for life-preserving abortions.

title: MeGee v. El Patio, LLC
description: Whether a commercial vendor or a bettor can be held liable for injuries or death sustained by a voluntarily intoxicated adult patron due to their own intoxication, either from being over-served alcohol or accepting a bet to drive while drunk.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argues that dram shop liability should extend to voluntarily intoxicated adults who injure themselves, especially given the egregious facts of being over-served and then bet to drive while intoxicated, and that betting an intoxicated person to drive is an actionable negligent act.
defendant_argument: The defendants argue that current Oklahoma law does not hold commercial vendors liable for injuries to voluntarily intoxicated adults due to their own intoxication, and that 'negligent betting' is not a recognized theory of liability.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's dismissal, ruling that a voluntarily intoxicated adult has no cause of action against a commercial vendor for self-inflicted injuries due to over-serving, nor against a bettor for injuries sustained while driving intoxicated after accepting a bet.

title: Kingfisher Wind, LLC v. Wehmuller
description: Whether Production Tax Credits (PTCs) utilized to finance the building of a wind farm are "property" which can be used to determine the fair cash value of the wind farm for ad valorem taxation purposes, with the plaintiff arguing they are intangible personal property exempt from taxation and the defendant arguing they are tangible property subject to taxation or should be included in valuation.
plaintiff_argument: Kingfisher Wind argued that Production Tax Credits (PTCs) are intangible personal property and are therefore not subject to ad valorem taxation under the Oklahoma Constitution.
defendant_argument: The County Assessors argued that Production Tax Credits (PTCs) are tangible personal property or are such an economic benefit that they must be included to determine the fair cash value of the wind farm for ad valorem taxation.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's decision, holding that Production Tax Credits (PTCs) are intangible personal property and are not subject to ad valorem taxation, and that the trial court's valuation findings were not against the weight of the evidence.

title: Ritter v. State
description: Whether Senate Bill 658, which restricts local school districts' ability to implement mask mandates without a gubernatorial emergency declaration, constitutes an unconstitutional delegation of legislative authority.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that Senate Bill 658 was unconstitutional because it restricted local school districts' control over public health decisions, specifically mask mandates, and constituted an impermissible delegation of legislative authority.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that Senate Bill 658 was constitutional and enforceable, defending the state's authority to impose restrictions on local school districts regarding health measures.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the provision in Senate Bill 658 requiring a gubernatorial emergency declaration for local school districts to implement mask mandates was an unconstitutional delegation of legislative authority and struck that specific clause, upholding the remainder of the statutes.

title: Hudson v. State (In re K. H.)
description: Whether the trial court abused its discretion by admitting evidence of pending criminal child abuse charges and including them in jury instructions during a parental rights termination trial.
plaintiff_argument: The parents argued that the admission of evidence of pending criminal charges and their inclusion in jury instructions was irrelevant, highly prejudicial, and violated their right to a fair trial.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the evidence of criminal charges was relevant to prove deprived adjudication and that any prejudice was mitigated by the jury instruction, and the dissent argued any error was harmless due to overwhelming evidence of abuse.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the judgments terminating parental rights and remanded the case for a new trial.
